section_summary: The section begins with State Department correspondence about textile supplies, cotton imports, rayon terminology, and travel costs for a textile mission to Japan. Most pages contain the mission’s March 1946 report, which estimates Japan’s textile capacity and inventories, examines shortages and damaged machinery, and recommends controls on new machinery production. The report continues beyond page 309.

subfiles.title: Closing page of earlier correspondence
subfiles.about: The surviving page closes a letter whose subject is on preceding pages.
subfiles.summary: Only a closing and filing marks are legible.

subfiles.title: Expenses and supplies for Bunce’s staff
subfiles.about: Sets payment, per diem, transportation, and supply arrangements for Bunce’s staff in Korea.
subfiles.summary: Explains salary and per diem charges, meal and lodging deductions, equipment shipments, and Miss Hayes’s possible assistance.

subfiles.title: Fred Taylor’s travel authorization
subfiles.about: Authorizes Taylor to investigate the cotton industry in China and Manchuria after his Japan mission.
subfiles.summary: Confirms the February 8 travel order and specifies the expense account.

subfiles.title: Korean patents and Japanese business property
subfiles.about: Requests views on Korean patent and trademark law and the disposition of Japanese business property.
subfiles.summary: The Department seeks background on ownership and concentration of industrial and commercial control in Korea.

subfiles.title: Reply on Japanese textile waste
subfiles.about: Replies to Reis’s inquiry about buying textile waste in Japan.
subfiles.summary: No waste is currently available for export; future sales to the United States would go through the U.S. Commercial Company.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about stocks of textile waste
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention E. M. Martin
subfiles.about: Asks whether occupation authorities have reported on Japanese stocks of textile waste.
subfiles.summary: Follows up on earlier correspondence about purchasing textile waste.

subfiles.title: Embroidery machinery purchase inquiry
subfiles.about: Redirects an inquiry about purchasing embroidery machinery from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Martin says Isabelle Ward is not in his division and forwards the inquiry to the Department of Commerce.

subfiles.title: Suggested letter on Japanese cotton imports
subfiles.about: Submits a suggested letter to the Secretary of Agriculture on Japanese cotton imports.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the Department’s proposed position on cotton imports.

subfiles.title: Thorp’s note on the cotton-import question
subfiles.about: Suggests writing to the Department of Agriculture about the developing cotton-import issue.
subfiles.summary: Thorp warns that the matter may grow difficult to manage.

subfiles.title: State Department position on cotton for Japan
subfiles.about: Explains why sources of Japan’s cotton imports require interagency and Allied consultation.
subfiles.summary: The initial plan relies on U.S. cotton, but Allied suppliers also seek access. Byrnes says MacArthur should not determine import sources alone and expects Far Eastern Commission review.

subfiles.title: Rayon definitions and Japanese industry reports
subfiles.about: Urges consistent rayon terminology in reports on Japan’s textile industry.
subfiles.summary: Rose explains that Japanese usage confuses rayon yarn with rayon generally, and asks Martin to circulate standard definitions.

subfiles.title: Copy of Rose’s letter to Major Tate
subfiles.about: Sends standard rayon definitions to SCAP’s Textile Branch.
subfiles.summary: Rose promises a standards book and notes that other U.S. offices will receive the definitions.

subfiles.title: Definitions of rayon terms
subfiles.to: E. M. Martin and Major I. S. Tate
subfiles.about: Defines fibre, rayon, rayon filament, rayon yarn, rayon staple, and spun rayon yarn.
subfiles.summary: A six-item terminology list distinguishes rayon products and their manufacture.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of rayon definitions
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Rose’s corrected fibre definitions and letter to SCAP.
subfiles.summary: Martin says the material has been circulated to State Department staff and interested divisions.

subfiles.title: Reimbursement for foreign delegates’ air travel
subfiles.from: C. C. Green, Army Service Forces
subfiles.to: Department of State, Special War Problems Division
subfiles.about: Requests collection of $2,730 for three foreign textile delegates’ travel to Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Lists Winterbottom, Bharat Ram, and Barekh and asks State to secure reimbursement from the British Government.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of travel reimbursement letter
subfiles.from: C. C. Green, Army Service Forces
subfiles.about: Duplicates the request for reimbursement of foreign delegates’ travel.
subfiles.summary: A degraded copy repeats the delegates’ names and travel route; page 250 is largely illegible.

subfiles.title: Invitational travel orders for textile delegates
subfiles.about: Authorizes delegates’ travel to Tokyo to advise the Supreme Commander on textile facilities.
subfiles.summary: The damaged copy records invited travel by military air transport.

subfiles.title: Digest of the Textile Mission report
subfiles.about: Summarizes the mission’s principal findings on Japanese textile capacity and shortages.
subfiles.summary: Covers cotton, rayon, wool, cloth stocks, machinery controls, and food-related labor shortages.

subfiles.title: Routing note for Textile Mission report
subfiles.about: Notes circulation of the Textile Mission report.
subfiles.summary: A short handwritten routing note, partly illegible.

subfiles.title: Report of Textile Mission to Japan, January–March 1946
subfiles.from: Fred Taylor, for the Textile Mission
subfiles.to: Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s ability to produce textiles in 1946–47, especially cotton goods for export.
subfiles.summary: The mission reports severe wartime losses of spinning and weaving equipment, but expects imported cotton and repairs to raise output. It surveys rayon, wool, silk, flax, clothing inventories, raw-material needs, and the possible export surplus. Machinery manufacture is complicated by reparations and Japan’s war potential; the mission recommends strict SCAP control of new equipment until production levels are settled. Page 309 begins its discussion of mill supplies, and the report continues after this section.
